{{Short description|Rendezvous problem variant}}
The '''deterministic rendezvous problem''' is a variant of the [[rendezvous problem]] where the players, or ''robots'', must find each other by following a [[determinism#Mathematical models|deterministic]] sequence of instructions. Although each robot follows the same instruction sequence, a unique label assigned to each robot is used for [[symmetry breaking]]. Typically, the robots act synchronously, though non-synchronous versions of the deterministic rendezvous problem exist.<ref name="Ta-Shma 2014">{{cite journal|last1=Ta-Shma|first1=Amnon|last2=Zwick|first2=Uri|author2-link=Uri Zwick|title=Deterministic rendezvous, treasure hunts, and strongly universal exploration sequences|journal=ACM Transactions on Algorithms|date=April 2014|volume=10|issue=3|doi=10.1145/2601068|s2cid=10718957|at=12}}</ref>

== Overview ==
In the synchronous version of the deterministic rendezvous problem, both robots are initially placed at arbitrary [[vertex (graph theory)|nodes]] in a finite, connected, undirected [[graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]]. The size and structure of the graph is unknown to the robots.

The information known by a robot is as follows:
*''T'', the number of time steps since it has been activated
*''d'', the [[degree (graph theory)|degree]] of the node currently occupied by the robot
*''L'', the label of the robot (typically taking the form of a bit string)

To solve the deterministic rendezvous problem, both robots must be given a sequence of deterministic instructions which allow the robots to use their known information to find each other. The robots are considered to have found each other if they are both occupying the same node in the graph during the same time step.<ref name="Ta-Shma 2014"/>

== Solutions ==
{{expand section|date=December 2016}}
A number of algorithms exist to solve the deterministic rendezvous problem. Some of the solutions are listed below:

=== Dessmark et al. ===
{{expand section|date=December 2016}}
In 2006, Dessmark et al. presented a solution which solves the deterministic rendezvous problem in time proportional to <math display="inline">O\left(n^5\sqrt{\tau l}+n^{10}l\right)</math>, where:
*''n'' is the number of nodes in the graph
*''τ'' is the difference in activation time between the two robots
*''l'' is the length of the shorter of the labels of the robots

This solution is not ideal, since ''τ'' is an input parameter of the deterministic rendezvous problem and can therefore be arbitrarily large.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Dessmark|first1=A.|last2=Fraingnaud|first2=P.|last3=Kowalski|first3=D.|last4=Pelc|first4=A.|title=Deterministic rendezvous in graphs|journal=Algorithmica|date=2006|volume=46|issue=1|pages=69–96|doi=10.1007/s00453-006-0074-2|s2cid=22236305|url=http://edoc.mpg.de/get.epl?fid=35769&did=314448&ver=0}}</ref>

=== Kowalski and Malinowski ===
{{expand section|date=December 2016}}
In 2008, Kowalski and Malinowski presented a solution which solves the problem in <math display="inline">O\left(n^{15}+l^3\right)</math> time.<ref name="Kowalski 2008">{{cite journal|last1=Kowalski|first1=D.|last2=Malinowski|first2=A.|title=How to meet in anonymous network|journal=Theoretical Computer Science|date=2008|volume=399|issue=1–2|pages=144–156|doi=10.1016/j.tcs.2008.02.010|doi-access=free}}</ref> This is a significant improvement, since this [[time complexity]] is not dependent on ''τ''. This solution has one major drawback, though. It makes use of ''backtracking'', where the robots must keep track of each edge that they have traversed. This is a drawback because it places assumptions on the structure of the graph (namely, how it is labeled), and the robots' sensory and memory capabilities.

=== Ta-Shma and Zwick ===
The solution presented by Ta-Shma and [[Uri Zwick|Zwick]] in 2014 solves the problem in <math display="inline">O\left(n^{5}+l\right)</math> time. In addition to the reduced time complexity (which doesn't rely on ''τ''), this solution also doesn't use [[backtracking]]. Instead, it uses the notion of [[graph traversal#Universal Traversal Sequences|universal traversal sequences]] to help solve the problem.<ref name="Ta-Shma 2014" />

A universal traversal sequence is a sequence of instructions comprising a [[graph traversal]] for any [[regular graph]] with a set number of vertices and for any starting vertex.<ref name="Aleliunas 1979">{{cite book|last1=Aleliunas|first1=R.|last2=Karp|first2=R.|last3=Lipton|first3=R.|last4=Lovász|first4=L.|last5=Rackoff|first5=C. |title=20th Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (SFCS 1979) |chapter=Random walks, universal traversal sequences, and the complexity of maze problems |date=1979|pages=218–223|doi=10.1109/SFCS.1979.34|s2cid=18719861}}</ref> Since the robots may not be in a regular graph, a universal traversal sequence for ''n'' nodes and degree ''d'' is used, where ''d'' is the maximum degree of the graph. Any instructions in the chosen universal traversal sequence which specify that the robot travels to a neighbor of the current node which doesn't exist (i.e., the current node has degree < ''d'') are ignored. By doing this, all nodes in the graph with degree less than ''d'' are treated as having enough self-loops to bring their total degree up to ''d'', effectively allowing the graph to be treated as regular for the purpose of universal traversals.<ref name="Ta-Shma 2014" />

The basic idea of Ta-Shma and Zwick's solution is that if one of the robots completes a complete traversal of the graph while the other robot remains idle, or ''rests'', then the two robots are guaranteed to meet. Since the size of the graph is unknown, the robots run universal traversal sequences for increasing values of ''n'', while periodically resting. Whether a robot rests before or after a traversal depends upon the value of its label.<ref name="Ta-Shma 2014" />

For example, one of the robots could run the sequence:
<math display="block">U_10^{u_1}U_20^{u_2}U_40^{u_4}U_80^{u_8}...U_{2^i}0^{u_{2^i}}...</math>
while the other robot runs the sequence:
<math display="block">0^{u_1}U_10^{u_2}U_20^{u_4}U_40^{u_8}U_8...0^{u_{2^i}}U_{2^i}...</math>
where U<sub>i</sub> is a universal traversal sequence for a graph with ''i'' nodes, u<sub>i</sub> is the number of steps in that universal traversal sequence, and 0<sup>k</sup> represents ''k'' steps where the robot rests. The universal traversal sequence for the size of the actual graph will be run by one robot while the other rests for the number of steps in that traversal. However, this only works if the two robots are activated at the same time.<ref name="Ta-Shma 2014" />

To cover the case where the robots are activated at different times, the sequence to run will include rest periods of length u<sub>i</sub> after each step (in the traversal and the rest period). For example, one of the robots would run the sequence:
<math display="block">\sigma_10^{u_1-1}\sigma_20^{u_1-1}\sigma_30^{u_1-1}...\sigma_{u_1}0^{u_1-1}0^{2u_1}\pi_10^{u_2-1}\pi_20^{u_2-1}\pi_30^{u_2-1}...\pi_{u_2}0^{u_2-1}0^{2u_2}</math>
where σ<sub>i</sub> is the ''i''<sup>th</sup> step of U<sub>1</sub> and π<sub>i</sub> is the ''i''<sup>th</sup> step of U<sub>2</sub>.<ref name="Ta-Shma 2014" />

In order to formally present the sequence that each robot will run, some additional notation is needed. Let:
*σ<sup>b</sup> = 0 if ''b'' = 0
*σ<sup>b</sup> = σ if ''b'' = 1
*<math>\bar{L} = 1 - L</math>
*<math>\sigma^{m_1..m_k}=\sigma_1^m...\sigma_k^m</math>
*<math>D_k(\sigma_1...\sigma_m)=\sigma_10^k...\sigma_m0^k</math>

Assuming that one robot's label is 0 and that the other robot's label is 1, the sequence that each robot would run is:
<math display="block">D_{u_1-1}((U_1U_1)^{L\bar{L}})D_{u_2-1}((U_2U_2)^{L\bar{L}})...D_{u_{2^k}-1}((U_{2^k}U_{2^k})^{L\bar{L}})...</math>

The sub-sequence <math display="inline">D_{u_i-1}((U_iU_i)^{L\bar{L}})</math> is known as a ''block'' and can be rewritten as <math display="inline">D_{u_i-1}((U_iU_i)^L(U_iU_i)^{\bar{L}})</math>.

If σ = U<sub>i</sub> and m = u<sub>i</sub>, the block can be further simplified to:
<math display="block">(\sigma_10^{m-1}...\sigma_m0^{m-1}\sigma_10^{m-1}...\sigma_m0^{m-1})^L</math>
<math display="block">(\sigma_10^{m-1}...\sigma_m0^{m-1}\sigma_10^{m-1}...\sigma_m0^{m-1})^{\bar{L}}</math>
Both of the above lines are known as ''chunks''. One chunk consists of a universal traversal sequence with interleaved rest periods, while the other chunk is a rest period of length 2''m''<sup>2</sup>.

If the robot's label is 0, then each block it runs is equal to:
<math display="block">0^{2m^2}\sigma_10^{m-1}...\sigma_m0^{m-1}\sigma_10^{m-1}...\sigma_m0^{m-1}</math>
If the label is 1, then each block it runs is equal to:
<math display="block">\sigma_10^{m-1}...\sigma_m0^{m-1}\sigma_10^{m-1}...\sigma_m0^{m-1}0^{2m^2}</math>

====Analysis====
{{expand section|date=December 2016}}
The sequence of instructions listed above will allow two robots with labels 0 and 1 to meet after O(''n''<sup>2c</sup>) time steps.<ref name="Ta-Shma 2014" />

Ta-Shma and Zwick show how to extend this solution to allow the robots to meet after only O(''n''<sup>c</sup>) time steps and how to deal with arbitrary labels (which increases the time until the robots meet to O(''n''<sup>5</sup>+''l'') time steps).<ref name="Ta-Shma 2014" />
